Audience

  • The intended audience for this paper includes sales engineers, field consultants, IT administrators, customers, and anyone who is interested in configuring Red Hat OpenStack Services on OpenShift with PowerFlex as the underlying software-defined storage.

    Readers are expected to have an understanding of:

    • Networking and storage basics
    • Red Hat Enterprise Linux operating system
    • OpenShift Container Platform
    • OpenStack
    • PowerFlex

Conclusion

  • This white paper presents the logical architecture and network design principles for deploying Red Hat OpenStack Services on OpenShift 18.0, leveraging Dell PowerFlex as the storage backend.

    The integration of Red Hat OpenStack with PowerFlex delivers a robust, high-performance solution tailored for organizations that are aiming to advance both containerization and private cloud capabilities. By uniting the scalability and adaptability of OpenStack with the software-defined storage strength of PowerFlex, enterprises can optimize efficiency, resilience, and agility across compute and storage layers.

    Red Hat OpenStack Services on OpenShift offers a comprehensive platform for building and sustaining modern, enterprise-grade private cloud environments. The solution further empowers IT teams with unified management of containerized workloads through a single-pane interface. This solution enables organizations to accelerate innovation while maintaining the reliability and performance essential to meet evolving business and operational demands. To find out more, contact your Dell sales representative.

Control plane deployment

  • Prerequisites

    Before deploying the RHOSO control plane, ensure that the following requirements are met for the specified components.

    RedHat OpenShift Container Platform cluster

    • Ensure that RHOCP is up and running. For more information about RHOCP deployment, see Installing OpenShift Container Platform with the Assisted Installer.
      • This solution uses a three-node compact RHOCP cluster. For the minimum hardware requirements, see Hardware configurations of control plane nodes.
      • Verify that all the RHOCP cluster operators are up and healthy.

    Preparing the admin VM

    • Ensure that you are logged in as a user with cluster-admin privileges.
    • Ensure that the oc client utility is installed on the admin VM to manage the RHOCP cluster using the kubeconfig file.

    Storage requirements for OpenStack services

    • Ensure that a 150 GB minimum persistent volume pool is available to store service logs, databases, file import conversion, and services metadata. This pool is backed by NFS shares which are mounted on all OCP nodes and the data plane nodes.
    • Ensure that separate directories are available for the required OpenStack services on the NFS shares mounted on the admin VM. To create the different directories:
      1. Create required directories in the NFS share. See Creating NFS shares for the required directories.
      2. Set the following permission on the directories you create to ensure read, write and execute permissions are given:

        chmod -R 775 *

      3. Add the respective directory entries in the /etc/exports file to allow control plane and data plane nodes to access the NFS share directories
    • Export the NFS share using the following command: sudo exportfs -a
    • Verify that the NFS share is accessible from each of the OCP nodes using the following command: showmount -e <NFS_SHARE_IP>

Control plane deployment

  • Control plane deployment steps

    Control plane deployment involves multiple operator installations and different configurations. The deployment consists of the following steps:

    • Operator installation
    • OpenStack namespace and secret creation
    • Control plane network configuration
    • Control plane storage configuration
    • Control plane Custom Resource (CR) creation

    Operator installation:

    Operators are used to provide infrastructure services and manage OpenStack components. The following operators are installed on the RHOCP cluster nodes:

    • NMState
    • MetalLB
    • Cert-manager
    • Cluster Observability
    • OpenStack Operator
    NMState operator manages and automates network configuration across OpenShift cluster nodes using the declarative approach. To install the NMState operator:
    1. Create an NMState operator namespace yaml file: 
      apiVersion: v1
      kind: Namespace
      metadata:
        labels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: openshift-nmstate
          name: openshift-nmstate
        name: openshift-nmstate
      spec:
        finalizers:
        - Kubernetes
    2. Create an NMState namespace using the following command:
      oc create -f nmstate_ns.yaml
    3. Create an NMState OperatorGroup yaml file: 
      apiVersion: operators.coreos.com/v1
      kind: OperatorGroup
      metadata:
        annotations:
          olm.providedAPIs: NMState.v1.nmstate.io
          name: openshift-nmstate
          namespace: openshift-nmstate
        spec:
          targetNamespaces:
                - openshift-nmstate
    4. Create an NMState OperatorGroup using the following command:: 
      oc create -f nmstate-og.yaml
    5. Create an nmstate-subscription.yaml file: 
      apiVersion: operators.coreos.com/v1alpha1
      kind: Subscription
      metadata:
        labels:
          operators.coreos.com/kubernetes-nmstate-operator.openshift-nmstate: ""
        name: kubernetes-nmstate-operator
        namespace: openshift-nmstate
      spec:
        channel: stable
        installPlanApproval: Automatic
        name: kubernetes-nmstate-operator
        source: red hat-operators
        sourceNamespace: openshift-marketplace
    6. Create an NMState subscription using the following command: 
      oc create -f nmstate-subscription.yaml
    7. Create an NMState operator instance yaml file: 
      apiVersion: nmstate.io/v1
      kind: NMState
      metadata:
        name: nmstate
    8. Create an NMState operator instance using the following command:
      oc create -f nmstate-instance.yaml
    9. Verify that the NMState operator is installed properly using by running the following command: 
      oc get clusterserviceversion -n openshift-nmstate \
      -o custom-columns=Name:.metadata.name,Phase:.status.phase

    While the preceding steps are focused on NMState operator, the installation of other operators, such as MetalLB, Cert-manager, Cluster Observability Operator, and OpenStack Operator, follows the same approach. For more information about operators, see RHOCP Software requirements.


    Create the OpenStack namespace and secrets

    1. Create the openstack project for deploying the RHOSO environment:
      oc new-project openstack
    2. Ensure that the openstack namespace is labeled to enable privileged pod creation by the OpenStack operators: 
      oc get namespace openstack -ojsonpath='{.metadata.labels}' | jq
      Expected output: 
      {
        		"kubernetes.io/metadata.name": "openstack",
        		"pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce": "privileged",
      "security.openshift.io/scc.podSecurityLabelSync": "false"
      }
      If the security context constraint (SCC) is not "privileged", use the following commands to change it: 
      oc label ns openstack security.openshift.io/scc.podSecurityLabelSync=false 
      --overwrite
      oc label ns openstack pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=privileged –overwrite
    3. Set the default namespace to openstack using the following command to avoid providing a namespace every time: 
      oc project openstack
    4. Create a secret custom resource to provide secure access to RHOSO service pods:
      1. Create a secret CR file openstack-service-secret.yaml.

        See Providing secure access to the Red Hat OpenStack Services on OpenShift services for the steps.

      2. Run the following command to create the secret and verify its creation: 
        oc create -f openstack-service-secret.yaml
        oc describe secret osp-secret -n openstack

    Control plane network configuration

    For a successful RHOSO deployment, configure the RHOCP networks on the RHOCP cluster. To configure the networks for control plane nodes:
    1. Verify that the worker nodes are up and running in the RHOCP cluster. 
      oc get nodes -l node-role.kubernetes.io/worker -o jsonpath="{.items[*].metadata.name}"

      ocpnode1.rhoso.com 
      ocpnode2.rhoso.com 
      ocpnode3.rhoso.com
      Note: This solution is deployed on a compact OpenShift cluster, where control plane and worker node roles are co-located on the same set of nodes.

    2. Create a NodeNetworkConfigurationPolicy (nncp) configuration file for each node, where nncp is used to configure the interfaces on each worker node of the RHOCP cluster to isolate different networks.
      1. In this solution, bond network configuration is used. The following command creates the bond configuration file for the OCP cluster:
        oc create -f bond1-config.yaml

        See Sample bond1-config.yaml . These steps create a bond between two physical NICs of the OCP cluster nodes.

      2. Create an nncp configuration file for each worker node to define different VLANs. For the steps for creating the file, see Preparing RHOCP with isolated network interfaces. Use the following command to create nncp CR: 
        oc create -f vlan-tagging-bond1-node1.yaml
        oc create -f vlan-tagging-bond1-node2.yaml
        oc create -f vlan-tagging-bond1-node3.yaml
    3. The NetworkAttachmentDefinition (NAD) CR is used to define isolated network for attaching the service pods. It enables pods to communicate with the different networks. See Attaching service pods to the isolated networks for the steps for creating a NAD CR definition file.
      1. Use the following command to create the NAD CR:
        oc create -f openstack-nad.yaml
      2. Verify the creation of NAD CR using the following command:
        oc get network-attachment-definitions -n openstack
    4. Create the IPAddressPool CR for managing the static IP addresses of the pods across the cluster. See Preparing RHOCP for RHOSO network VIPS for the steps for creating the IPAddressPool CR definition file.
      1. Use the following command to create the IPAddressPool CR:
        oc apply -f openstack-ipaddresspools.yaml
      2. Verify IPAddressPool CR creation using the following command:
        oc describe -n metallb-system IPAddressPool
    5. Create an L2Advertisement CR to manage how IP addresses are advertised on the local Layer 2 network. This file helps direct the external traffic to the correct node in the cluster using LoadBalancerIP. See Preparing RHOCP for RHOSO network VIPS for the steps for creating the L2Advertisement CR definition file.
      1. Use the following command to create the L2Advertisement CR:
        oc apply -f openstack-l2advertisement.yaml
      2. Verify L2Advertisement creation using the following command: 
        oc describe -n metallb-system L2Advertisement
    6. Create the NetConfig CR to define all subnet and IP allocation range for the data plane networks. This CR is an important component that is used to define and orchestrate the networking layout for OpenStack services. For the steps for creating the openstacknetconfig CR definition file, see Creating the data plane network.
      1. Create openstacknetconfig CR using the following command:
        oc apply -f openstack-netconfig.yaml -n openstack
      2. Verify openstacknetconfig CR creation using the following command:
        oc get netconfig -n openstack

      If any errors occur during creation of the NetConfig file, verify the underlying NetworkAttachedDefination(NAD) and NodeNetworkConfigurationPolicy(nncp) custom resources to ensure the proper network configurations are defined across control and data plane networks.

      Use the following command for verification:

      oc get network-attachment-definitions -n openstack
      oc get nncp

    For more information about networks, see Preparing networks for RHOSO.


    Preparing the storage for the deployment

    It is necessary to create persistent volume pools created for each service to store service logs, databases, file import conversion, and metadata. The NFS share is created as a storage backend for the Persistent Volume pools. See Storage requirements for OpenStack services for the NFS configuration.

    To provision the storage for control plane pods:

    1. Create a storage class file to provide persistent volume RHOSO control plane pods:
      kind: StorageClass
      apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
      metadata:
        name: local-storage
      provisioner: kubernetes.io/no-provisioner
      volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
    2. Create a storage class using the following command:
      oc create -f openstack-local-storage-class.yaml
    3. Verify storage class creation using the following command: 
      oc get sc
    4. Create Persistent Volumes for each of the control plane pods:
      1. Create Persistent Volumes using the following command:
        oc create -f openstack-persistent-volumes-ctlplane.yaml
        See the openstack-persistent-volumes-ctlplane.yaml sample file for reference.
      2. Verify the persistent volumes creation using the following command:
        oc get pv

    Creating the control plane

    The OpenStackContolPlane CR file is defined to perform tasks such as creating the control plane, enabling the required Red Hat OpenStack services, configuring the control plane network, and configuring service backends.

    To create the file:
    1. Add the required service configuration, such as block-storage service (Cinder), compute-service (Nova), DNS service, Identity service(Keystone), image service (Glance), and so on, in the control plane CR file.
    2. Specify the created secret details to provide secure access to the RHOSO environment.
    3. Specify the created storage class details to provide the storage backend.
    4. Add MariaDB Galera, Memcached and RabbitMQ service details to implement the HA for the control plane services.
    5. See Example OpenStackControlPlane CR to create the OpenStackControlPlane CR file. Create the OpenStackControlPlane using the following command 
      oc create -f openstack-control-plane.yaml
    6. Verify control plane installation using the following command: 
      oc get openstackcontrolplanes
    7. Confirm the successful deployment of control plane by verifying that all the required control plane pods are in a Running state within the OpenStack namespace. 
      oc get pods -n openstack
    For detailed information about control plane deployment, see Creating the control plane.

Data plane deployment

  • Prerequisites

    This solution uses pre-provisioned nodes for data plane deployment. Before deploying the RHOSO data plane, ensure that the following prerequisites are met:

    • A functional control plane created using he OpenStack operator is installed.
    • At least two nodes with RHEL 9.4 are installed.
    • A routable IP address is available on the control plane network to enable Ansible access over SSH to the data plane nodes.
    • A cloud-admin user exists on the nodes. Ensure that you add the user to the sudoers file so that it is a passwordless login.
    • Ensure that the following details are added to the /opt/emc/scaleio/openstack/connector.conf on the data plane nodes:
      [powerflex]
      san_password = <SAN_PASSWORD>

    Before starting the data plane deployment, perform the following steps:

    • Create the SSH key and secrets.
    • Create a Persistent Volume.

    SSH key and secret creation

    Generate an SSH key pair to enable Ansible to securely manage the RHEL nodes within the data plane cluster.

    1. Create the SSH keypair in admin VM using the following command: 
      ssh-keygen -f id_rsa_edpm -N "" -t rsa -b 4096
    2. Copy the SSH key to each data plane node. For example: 
      ssh-copy-id -i id_rsa_edpm.pub cloud-admin@<edpm-compute node_name>
    3. Create and apply the secret using the following command. This secret is used to store the SSH credentials, which are used by Ansible to connect and manage the data plane nodes. 
      oc create secret generic dataplane-ansible-ssh-private-key-secret --save-config --dry-run=client --from-file=ssh-privatekey=id_rsa_edpm --from-file=ssh-publickey=id_rsa_edpm.pub -n openstack -o yaml | oc apply -f-
    4. Verify the secret: 
      oc describe secret dataplane-ansible-ssh-private-key-secret
    5. Create the SSH key pair, for instance migration using the following command: 
      ssh-keygen -f ./id -t ecdsa-sha2-nistp521 -N ''
    6. Create the respective secret CR, for instance, migration, and apply it to the cluster: 
      oc create secret generic nova-migration-ssh-key --from-file=ssh-privatekey=id --from-file=ssh-publickey=id.pub -n openstack -o yaml | oc apply -f-
      secret/nova-migration-ssh-key configured
    7. Verify that the secret is created: 
      oc describe secret nova-migration-ssh-key
    8. Encode the subscription manager credentials for the subscription manager secret using the following command: 
      echo -n "YourSubscriptionManagerUsername" | base64
      echo -n "YourSubscriptionManagerPassword" | base64
    9. Create the secret file for storing the subscription-manager credentials and add the encoded username and password you created in the preceding steps: 
      apiVersion: v1
      kind: Secret
      metadata:
        name: subscription-manager
        namespace: openstack
      data:
        username: dml2ZWthbmFuZGFuLmtAZGVsbC5jb20=
        password: Vml2ZWsxMDAxOTI=
    10. Create a subscription secret using the following command: 
      oc create -f secret-subscription.yaml
    11. Verify the subscription manager secret using the following command: 
      oc describe secret subscription-manager
    12. Create the secret to be used to store the Red Hat registry credentials: 
      oc create secret generic red hat-registry --from-literal edpm_container_registry_logins='{"registry.red hat.io": {"<username>": "<password>"}}'
    13. Create the libvirt secret file that is used to authenticate between compute service (nova) and provisioned virtual machines. Create a libvirt-secret.yaml file to define the libvirt secret: 
      apiVersion: v1
      data:
       LibvirtPassword: <base64_password>
      kind: Secret
      metadata:
       name: libvirt-secret
       namespace: openstack
      type: Opaque
    14. Create and verify the libvirt secret CR using the following command. 
      oc create -f libvirt-secret.yaml
      oc describe secret libvirt-secret

    Create Persistent Volume Claim for Ansible logs

    Use the following steps to create a Persistent Volume Claim in the OpenStack namespace to store the logs generated by the Ansible workflow:
    1. Create a persistent volume file using the local-storage (NFS share) StorageClass created during the control plane deployment: 
      openstack-ansible-pv.yaml
      kind: PersistentVolume
      apiVersion: v1
      metadata:
        name: dataplane-ansible-logs
        namespace: openstack
      spec:
        capacity:
          storage: 10Gi
        accessModes:
          - ReadWriteOnce
        local:
          path: /mnt/openstack/ansible-logs-pv
        claimRef:
          namespace: openstack
          name: dataplane-ansible-logs
        nodeAffinity:
          required:
            nodeSelectorTerms:
            - matchExpressions:
              - key: kubernetes.io/hostname
                operator: In
                values:
                - ocpnode1.rhoso.com
                - ocpnode2.rhoso.com
                - ocpnode3.rhoso.com
        persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Delete
        volumeMode: Filesystem
        storageClassName: local-storage
    2. Create a Persistent Volume for the Ansible workflow: 
      oc create -f openstack-ansible-pv.yaml
    3. Create an Ansible Persistent Volume Claim file to claim the persistent volumes you created in the preceding steps: 

      kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
      apiVersion: v1
      metadata:
        name: dataplane-ansible-logs
        namespace: openstack
      spec:
        accessModes:
          - ReadWriteOnce
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 10Gi
        volumeName: dataplane-ansible-logs
        storageClasseName: local-storage
        volumeMode: Filesystem
    4. Create the Persistent Volume Claim for the Ansible workflow: 
      oc create -f openstack-ansible-pvc.yaml
    5. Verify that the Persistent Volume Claim is created: 
      oc get pvc
    6. Create a local directory on each data plane nodes to serve as the mount point for the persistent volume: 
      ssh core@ocpnode1.rhoso.com "sudo mkdir -p /mnt/openstack/ansible-logs-pv"
      ssh core@ocpnode2.rhoso.com "sudo mkdir -p /mnt/openstack/ansible-logs-pv"
      ssh core@ocpnode3.rhoso.com "sudo mkdir -p /mnt/openstack/ansible-logs-pv"

Data plane deployment

  • Data plane deployment steps

    Data plane deployment comprises the following two steps:

    • Creating the data plane nodeset CR
    • Deploying the data plane deployment CR

    Data plane nodeset CR creation

    The OpenStackDataPlaneNodeSet CR defines the nodes and layout of the data plane. Each node set can be connected to only one compute cell. By default, node sets are connected to cell1. If you customize your control plane to include additional compute cells, you must specify the cell to which the NodeSet is connected.

    For more information about adding compute cells, see Connecting an OpenStackDataPlaneNodeSet CR to a Compute cell.

    Create the openstack-edpm-node-set.yaml CR file, which includes multiple sections. Sections with variable values are explained here:

    1. Create the required name for the NodeSet. This example uses openstack-data-plane name as the reference: 
      apiVersion: dataplane.openstack.org/v1beta1
      kind: OpenStackDataplaneNodeSet
      metadata:
        name: openstack-data-plane
        namespace: openstack
      spec:
        env:
          - name: ANSIBLE_FORCE_COLOR
            value: "True"
    2. Connect the data plane to the control plane network: 
      spec:
        ...
        networkAttachments:
          - ctlplane
    3. This solution uses a pre-provisioned node, so specify the value as true for this parameter: 
      ..
      preProvisioned: true
      ...
    4. Add the SSH key secret you created previously to enable Ansible to connect to the data plane nodes: 
      … <truncated>
      nodeTemplate:
          ansibleSSHPrivateKeySecret: dataplane-ansible-ssh-private-key-secret
      … <truncated>
    5. The following parameter enables the mount point path for storing the ansible playbook logs. Update the extraMounts parameter with the PVC created for Ansible logs during the data plane deployment: 
      extraMounts:
            - extraVolType: Logs
              volumes:
              - name: ansible-logs
                persistentVolumeClaim:
                  claimName: dataplane-ansible-logs
              mounts:
              - name: ansible-logs
                mountPath: "/runner/artifacts"
    6. Specify the management network: 
      nodeTemplate:
          ...
          managementNetwork: ctlplane
    7. Update the secret parameter with the secret name you created during the data plane deployment: 
      ansible:
            ansibleUser: cloud-admin
            ansiblePort: 22
            ansibleVarsFrom:
              - prefix: subscription_manager_
                secretRef:
                  name: subscription-manager
              - secretRef:
                  name: red hat-registry
    8. Update the Red Hat subscription details to register the data plane nodes and enable the required repositories to ensure access to the necessary packages: 
      edpm_bootstrap_command: |
                subscription-manager register --username {{ “subscription_manager_username” }} --password {{ “subscription_manager_password” }}
                subscription-manager release --set=9.4
                subscription-manager repos --disable=*
                subscription-manager repos --enable=rhel-9-for-x86_64-baseos-eus-rpms --enable=rhel-9-for-x86_64-appstream-eus-rpms --enable=rhel-9-for-x86_64-highavailability-eus-rpms --enable=fast-datapath-for-rhel-9-x86_64-rpms --enable=rhoso-18.0-for-rhel-9-x86_64-rpms --enable=rhceph-7-tools-for-rhel-9-x86_64-rpms
    9. Specify a name, IP address, and network details for each node: 
      … <truncated>
      	nodes:
            edpm-compute1:
              hostName: edpm-compute1
              ansible:
                ansibleHost: <IP address that Ansible uses to connect to the node1>
              networks:
              - name: CtlPlane
                subnetName: subnet1
                defaultRoute: false
                fixedIP: 172.17.163.90  # predictable IP from address NetConfig CR
              - name: InternalApi
                subnetName: subnet1
              - name: Storage
                subnetName: subnet1
              - name: Tenant
                subnetName: subnet1
            edpm-compute2:
              hostName: edpm-compute2
              ansible:
                ansibleHost: <IP address that Ansible uses to connect to the node2>
              networks:
              - name: CtlPlane
                subnetName: subnet1
                defaultRoute: false
                fixedIP: 172.17.163.91 # predictable IP from address NetConfig CR
              - name: InternalApi
                subnetName: subnet1
              - name: Storage
                subnetName: subnet1
              - name: Tenant
                subnetName: subnet1
      … <truncated
    10. Update the NTP server IP: 
      edpm_chrony_ntp_servers:
                - 172.17.170.5
    11. Update the MAC address of the NIC used to configure the OpenStack Network the data plane nodes: 
    ansibleVars:
         edpm_network_config_os_net_config_mappings:
              edpm-compute1:
                # Map nic1 to eno1/enp1s0f0
                nic1: "xx:xx:xx:xx:xx:xx"
              edpm-compute2:
                # Map nic1 to eno1/enp1s0f0
                nic1: "xx:xx:xx:xx:xx:xx"
    1. Add the network configuration template for data plane nodes. The following example applies the single NIC VLANs network configuration to the data plane nodes. Choose the required template from Customizing data plane networks and configure the template accordingly based on your network configuration: 
      ---
        {% set mtu_list = [ctlplane_mtu] %}
        {% for network in nodeset_networks %}
        {{ mtu_list.append(lookup('vars', networks_lower[network] ~ '_mtu')) }}
        {%- endfor %}
        {% set min_viable_mtu = mtu_list | max %}
        network_config:
        - type: ovs_bridge
          name: {{ neutron_physical_bridge_name }}
          mtu: {{ min_viable_mtu }}
          use_dhcp: false
          dns_servers: {{ ctlplane_dns_nameservers }}
          domain: {{ dns_search_domains }}
          addresses:
          - ip_netmask: {{ ctlplane_ip }}/{{ ctlplane_cidr }}
          routes: {{ ctlplane_host_routes }}
          members:
          - type: interface
            name: nic1
            mtu: {{ min_viable_mtu }}
            #force the MAC address of the bridge to this interface
            primary: true
        {% for network in nodeset_networks %}
          - type: vlan
            mtu: {{ lookup('vars', networks_lower[network] ~ '_mtu') }}
            vlan_id: {{ lookup('vars', networks_lower[network] ~ '_vlan_id') }}
            addresses:
            - ip_netmask:
                {{ lookup('vars', networks_lower[network] ~ '_ip') }}/{{ lookup('vars', networks_lower[network] ~ '_cidr') }}
            routes: {{ lookup('vars', networks_lower[network] ~ '_host_routes') }}
        {% endfor %}
    2. Specify the NIC interface name used to communicate to data plane nodes during the deployment: 
      neutron_public_interface_name: eno2np1.170
    3. Add the following code snippet at the end of the CR file with the path of connector.conf file. This file contains the PowerFlex credentials which allow the compute resource to securely attach and detach volumes. 
      edpm_nova_extra_bind_mounts:
                  - src: /opt/emc/scaleio/openstack/connector.conf
                    dest: /opt/emc/scaleio/openstack/connector.conf
                    options: "ro"
    4. Save the data plane node set CR file openstack-edpm-node-set.yaml.
    5. Create an OpenStackDataplaneNodeSet CR using openstack-edpm-node-set.yaml file using the following command. See Sample openstack-edpm-node-set.yaml for reference. For more information, see Creating an OpenStackDataPlaneNodeSet CR with pre-provisioned nodes 
      oc create -f openstack-edpm-node-set.yaml –-save-config -n openstack
    6. Verify that the data plane resources have been created by confirming that the status is SetupReady: 
      oc get openstackdataplanenodeset
      Note:

      When the status is SetupReady, the command returns a condition met message; otherwise it returns a timeout with an error.



    7. Verify that the secret is created for the node set: 
      oc get secret | grep openstack-data-plane
    8. Verify that the data plane services is created: 
      oc get openstackdataplaneservice -n openstack

    Data plane deployment CR creation

    The OpenStackDataPlaneDeploymentCR triggers the Ansible playbook execution that deploys and configures the OpenStack services on the data plane nodes.

    1. Create the OpenStackDataplaneDeployment CR file by adding the nodeSet CR details: 
      openstack-edpm-deploy.yaml
      apiVersion: dataplane.openstack.org/v1beta1
      kind: OpenStackDataplaneDeployment
      metadata:
        name: openstack-edpm-deploy
        namespace: openstack
      spec:
        nodeSets:
          - <nodeSet_name>
    2. Deploy the data plane CR: 
      oc create -f openstack-edpm-deploy.yaml -n openstack
    3. View the Ansible logs by running the following command while deployment is in progress: 
      oc logs -l app=openstackansibleee -f --max-log-requests 100
    4. The deployment creates different deployment jobs. Verify the progress of those jobs by running the following command: 
      oc get pods  -l app=openstackansibleee
    5. Verify data plane deployment: 
      oc get openstackdataplanedeployment
      NAME                    NODESETS                   STATUS   MESSAGE
      openstack-edpm-deploy   ["openstack-data-plane"]   True     Setup complete
    6. Once the data plane deployment is successful, the openstackdataplanenodeset CR status also changes to NodeSet Ready. Verify this by running the following command: 
      oc get openstackdataplanenodesets
      NAME                   STATUS   MESSAGE
      openstack-data-plane   True     NodeSet Ready
    7. Connect to the Nova compute pod and verify the content of the connector.conf file: 
      oc rsh <nova_compute> -n openstack
      cat /opt/emc/scaleio/openstack/connector.conf 
      [powerflex]
      san_password = <SAN_PASSWORD>

Home > Storage > PowerFlex > White Papers > Red Hat OpenStack Services on OpenShift 18.0 with Dell PowerFlex > Logical architecture

Logical architecture

  • The following figure provides an overview of the logical architecture of RHOSO 18 with PowerFlex:

    The architecture consists of the following components:

    • Control plane nodes: RHOCP is deployed as a compact cluster on three bare metal nodes. The OpenStack operator is used to create control plane nodes on the OpenShift cluster. Along with OpenStack operator, additional operators are installed, such as NMState, Cert-manager, and MetalLB for managing compute, storage, and network resources. These operators are also used to configure the data plane, while control plane nodes handle orchestration, scheduling and overall resource management.
    • Data plane nodes: Three data plane nodes are configured. The data plane nodes are dedicated infrastructure components that run user workloads such as virtual machines, networking services, and storage operations. These nodes are defined and managed using OpenStackDataPlaneNodeSet custom resources, allowing tailored configurations for compute, network, or storage roles. Their primary objective is to deliver scalable, high-performance performance of services. The PowerFlex SDC is installed on all the data plane nodes which act as a block device driver. The SDC communicates with PowerFlex storage to provision storage volumes for the workload.

    The PowerFlex system is deployed in a two-layer configuration, consisting of four storage nodes. The system consists of the MDM, SDS, and LIA components. All the components are deployed automatically using PowerFlex Manager. A single PowerFlex protection domain with multiple storage pools is configured on PowerFlex.

    The Cinder service communicates with PowerFlex systems using the PowerFlex Manager IP as the REST endpoint to perform storage operations.

Map compute node to compute cell

  • Enable and verify Horizon access

    The OpenStack dashboard, Horizon, is the web-based UI that is used to manage OpenStack services. Perform the following steps to enable and verify Horizon access. Save the Horizon URL to perform different OpenStack operations.

    1. Obtain the OpenStackControlplane CR name using the following command: 
      oc get openstackcontrolplanes
      NAME                      STATUS   MESSAGE
      openstack-control-plane   True     Setup complete
    2. Enable the dashboard service in the OpenStackControlplane CR using the following command: 
      oc patch openstackcontrolplanes/openstack-control-plane -p='[{"op": "replace", "path": "/spec/horizon/enabled", "value": true}]' --type json
      openstackcontrolplane.core.openstack.org/openstack-control-plane patched
    3. Verify that the Horizon service is deployed using the following command: 
      oc get horizons horizon
      NAME      NETWORKATTACHMENTS   STATUS   MESSAGE
      horizon                        True     Setup complete
    4. Retrieve the dashboard service endpoint URL using the following command: 
      oc get horizons horizon -o jsonpath='{.status.endpoint}'
      https://horizon-openstack.apps.rhocp.rhoso.com
    5. Obtain the admin password from the osp-secret file using the following command: 
      oc get secret osp-secret -o jsonpath='{.data.AdminPassword}' | base64 -d
      Danger0us
    6. Log in and verify the Horizon dashboard:

Home > Storage > PowerFlex > White Papers > Red Hat OpenStack Services on OpenShift 18.0 with Dell PowerFlex > Network architecture

Network architecture

  • The following diagram shows the network architecture of this solution:

    At the physical layer, two supported TOR switches are used for redundancy and load balancing. A peer link is configured on both the TOR switches.

    Each PowerFlex storage-only node is connected to the TOR switches. The network ports are trunked with the TOR switches. The NICs handle management, data1, data2, data3, and data4 network traffic for PowerFlex. The management network operates in active-backup (mode1) bonding with the data1 and data2 networks, while the data3 and data4 networks are dedicated to the SDS network and are not bonded. This network configuration provides redundancy and fault tolerance, with two dedicated networks for PowerFlex data transfer. Dedicated VLANs are used to separate management and data network traffic.

    The following table shows the different VLANs that are used for PowerFlex SO nodes and their purposes:

     Table 3.  Network details for PowerFlex storage-only nodes  
    Network typeConfiguration
    ManagementMode1 bond (interface1 port1 and interface2 port1)
    PowerFlex Data 1Interface1 port1
    PowerFlex Data 2Interface2 port1
    PowerFlex Data 3Interface1 port2
    PowerFlex Data 4Interface2 port2

    Each OpenShift node is connected to TOR switches. The following port configuration specifies the network details for the OpenShift nodes:

    • Interface1 port1 and Interface2 port1: Combined and made bond and used for OpenShift Ingress/API network.
    • Interface1 port2 & Interface2 port2: Bonded with PowerFlex data networks. This bond is also used for OpenStack control plane networks.

    Each Data plane node is connected to TOR switches. The following port configuration specifies the network details for OpenStack data plane nodes:

    • Interface1 port1: Configured as native VLAN for OpenStack provision/control plane network.
    • Interface2 port2: Configured for differentOpenStack networks and identified with different VLANs. These networks are trunked with the TOR switches. In this solution, these networks are configured using a virtual bridge network configuration file. For more information about the network options available with the RHOSO environment, see Network interface configuration options.

Data networks are not bonded, and they carry dedicated SDS-SDC traffic. Data networks are used for communication between data plane nodes and PowerFlex storage nodes.

Network considerations

  • Network planning is important for successful deployment and operation of the RHOSO environment.

    At the physical layer, two top-of-rack (TOR) switches are configured to provide redundancy and load balancing. Depending on the switch vendor, either Virtual Link Trunking or Virtual Port Channel is configured. The required VLANs are created on the switches to separate the different network traffic types on the physical interfaces.

    The following table shows the list of networks used for the RHOSO deployment:

    Table 2. List of networks
    Network name Purpose
    IPMI Network used for power management of nodes.
    Provisioning Control planes use this network for deployment and management.
    Internal API This network is used for communication between the RHOSO services using API communication, RPC messages, and database communication.
    Tenant

    The networking service (neutron) provides each tenant (project) with their own networks using either:

    • VLAN separation

    or

    • Tunneling over VXLAN or GRE
    Storage A network used for block Storage, NFS, iSCSI, and other protocols. Ideally isolated for performance reasons.
    Storage Management OpenStack Object Storage (swift) uses this network to synchronize data objects between participating replica nodes.
    External

    Hosts the OpenStack Dashboard (Horizon) for graphical system management, and the public APIs for OpenStack services, and performs SNAT for incoming traffic that is destined for instances.

    Ensure that this network is accessible from control plane nodes.
    Ingress OpenShift Ingress configuration plays a vital role in enabling secure and scalable access to OpenStack services running inside the OpenShift cluster.

    RHOSO uses its own software-defined network service to automatically operate and manage different networks components.

    In a typical RHOSO deployment, the amount of logical network traffic always outnumbers the physical networks available on the nodes.

    For more information about Network considerations, see RHOSO network planning.

    Note: All networks that are mentioned in the preceding table are isolated networks. In addition, control plane networks are created automatically during control plane deployment using network configuration files.

Overview

  • In today’s rapidly evolving digital landscape, enterprises are encouraged to keep pace with technological advancements to remain competitive in the market. Cloud transformation, spanning private, public, and hybrid environments, is a driver of business agility, operational efficiency, and innovation. OpenStack has emerged as one of the leading open-source cloud platforms, widely adopted by enterprises and developers to power the digital infrastructure of an organization with flexibility and control. However, due to the breadth and complexity of its ecosystem, deploying and managing OpenStack can be challenging.

    To simplify this process and accelerate time to value, Dell Technologies and Red Hat have collaborated to deliver a validated solution that integrates Red Hat OpenStack Services on OpenShift (RHOSO) 18 with Dell PowerFlex software-defined infrastructure. This joint offering provides comprehensive guidance for the planning, deployment, and configuration of RHOSO with PowerFlex. The result is a robust, enterprise-grade hybrid cloud architecture that combines the open, modular capabilities of OpenStack with the high availability, performance, and advanced data services of PowerFlex. The unified approach lets organizations create scalable, resilient cloud infrastructures that support modern applications while streamlining infrastructure management. By leveraging native OpenStack platform alongside Dell’s software-defined infrastructure, IT teams can optimize resource utilization, improve operational efficiency, and reduce total cost of ownership. The combination of RHOSO 18 and PowerFlex empowers enterprises to confidently deploy private and hybrid cloud infrastructures that deliver consistent performance, data resiliency, and simplified management at scale.

PowerFlex overview

  • PowerFlex family

    PowerFlex software-defined infrastructure enables broad consolidation across the data center, encompassing most workloads. The software-first architecture enables automation and programmability of the complete infrastructure stack. PowerFlex provides scalability, performance, and resiliency to enable effortless adherence to stringent workload SLAs.

    The PowerFlex family provides a foundation that combines compute and high-performance storage resources in a managed unified fabric. PowerFlex comes in flexible consumption options (rack, appliance, custom nodes, or in the public cloud) that enable independent (disaggregated) architectures. PowerFlex is ideal for high-performance applications and databases, building an agile private/hybrid cloud, or consolidating resources in heterogeneous environments.

PowerFlex overview

  • PowerFlex software components

    Software is the key differentiation in the PowerFlex offering. PowerFlex software components not only provide the distributed software-defined storage services, but also help simplify infrastructure management and orchestration. The management software enables comprehensive IT Operational Management (ITOM) and Life Cycle Management (LCM) capabilities that span compute as well as storage infrastructure, from BIOS and Firmware to nodes, software, and networking.

    PowerFlex core software

    PowerFlex is a software-defined scale-out block storage service that is designed to deliver flexibility, elasticity, and simplicity with predictable high performance and resiliency at scale.

    For more information, see PowerFlex specifications.

    PowerFlex Manager

    PowerFlex Manager enables ITOM automation and LCM capabilities for PowerFlex systems. The unified PowerFlex Manager brings together three separate components from previous releases – PowerFlex Manager, the core PowerFlex UI, and the PowerFlex gateway. The PowerFlex UI runs in Kubernetes and embraces a modern development framework.

PowerFlex overview

  • PowerFlex deployment architectures

    PowerFlex software-defined storage can be deployed in disaggregated (independent compute and storage layers) architectures.

    Independent architecture

    In an independent or disaggregated architecture, some nodes provide storage capacity for data in applications, while other separate and independent nodes provide compute resources for applications and workloads. Compute and storage resources can be scaled independently by the addition of nodes to the cluster while it remains active. This separation of compute and storage resources helps minimize software licensing costs in certain situations. This architecture can be ideal for high-performance databases and application workloads.

    Disaggregation gives organizations the freedom to choose different LCM options that best align with their operational models. Not only can PowerFlex Manager manage the LCM of the PowerFlex storage infrastructure, it can also manage the LCM of PowerFlex compute nodes. Along with this freedom, there is also the choice to manage compute estates that connect to PowerFlex with other tooling; for example, VxRail Dynamic Nodes connected to PowerFlex using VxRail Manager automation.

PowerFlex overview

  • PowerFlex consumption options

    PowerFlex rack

    PowerFlex rack is a software-defined infrastructure platform that combines compute and high-performance storage resources in a managed unified network. This rack-based engineered system, with integrated networking, enables customers to achieve the scalability and management requirements of a modern data center.

    PowerFlex appliance

    PowerFlex appliance is a PowerEdge-based server which has been configured to be a node in a software-defined storage deployment that runs PowerFlex software components. This offering gives customers the flexibility and savings to bring their own compatible networking or make use of full network automation using a supported set of Dell or Cisco switches.

    PowerFlex custom nodes

    PowerFlex Custom Nodes are validated server building-blocks configured for use with PowerFlex. They are available with thousands of configuration options for customers who prefer to build their own environments.

    PowerFlex in the public cloud

    PowerFlex software storage services can be deployed on recommended instances (with attached storage) in Amazon Web Services or Microsoft Azure. Only the MG data layout and independent (disaggregated) architecture is supported. Fault Sets may be used to distribute the cluster across multiple Availability Zones (AZs), improving resiliency even during AZ disruptions. Native asynchronous replication may be used to migrate data between cloud and on-premises PowerFlex systems, or to establish cloud-based BC/DR data protection schemes.

PowerFlex overview

  • PowerFlex CSI/CSM 

    An important component outside PowerFlex that enables a flexible consumption model for Kubernetes is the PowerFlex CSI driver, developed as a part of the Dell Kubernetes strategy. After you load the CSI driver for PowerFlex into Kubernetes, you can use it to provision persistent volumes from the underlying PowerFlex storage resource. If the Kubernetes deployment is running low on PowerFlex storage resources, you can add PowerFlex storage nodes to increase the system capacity and performance.

    The CSI driver connects the PowerFlex system and Kubernetes deployments. It is a storage broker which dynamically provisions volumes from PowerFlex through the PowerFlex API gateway to the Kubernetes cluster. Once the volume is available on PowerFlex, it is immediately mapped to the requesting pod. If a pod is destroyed or rescheduled, the CSI plug-in ensures that the volumes are remapped upon rescheduling of that pod. 

    Customers running Kubernetes clusters on PowerFlex use the Dell Container Storage Modules (CSMs), which extend the CSI driver capabilities. These modules:

    • Provide enterprise storage capabilities to Kubernetes for cloud-native stateful applications.
    • Reduce management complexity, so that developers can independently use enterprise storage with ease and automate daily operations.
    • Extend storage functionality and capabilities beyond using the CSI driver alone.

    These modules include replication, observability, authorization, application mobility, and resiliency.

    PowerFlex supports multiple operating systems. PowerFlex is validated with the leading Kubernetes distributions, as shown in the following figure:

PowerFlex with RHOSO configuration

  • PowerFlex configuration in the control plane

    Configure PowerFlex as the storage backend in the OpenStackControlplane CR. To configure PowerFlex storage in the OpenStackControlplane custom resource:

    1. Create a secret file powerflex-secret.yaml and add the PowerFlex details, as shown in the following code extract: 
      apiVersion: v1
      kind: Secret
      metadata:
        labels:
          component: cinder-volume
          service: cinder
        name: cinder-volume-powerflex-secrets
      stringData:
        powerflex-secrets.conf: |
          [powerflex]
          san_ip=<powerflex_ip>
          san_login=admin
          san_password=<Password>
      type: Opaque
    2. Create the secret using the following command: 
      oc create -f powerflex-secret.yaml
    3. Verify the PowerFlex secret using the following command: 
      oc describe secret/cinder-volume-powerflex-secrets
    4. Create a secret file and add the PowerFlex password details, as shown in the following code extract: 
      apiVersion: v1
      kind: Secret
      metadata:
        labels:
          component: cinder-volume
          service: cinder
        name: powerflex-connector-conf-file
      stringData:
        connector.conf: |
          [powerflex]
          san_password=<Password>
      type: Opaque
    5. Create the connector secret using the following command: 
      oc create -f powerflex-connector-secret.yaml
    6. Verify that the connector configuration secret is created using the following command: 
      oc describe secret/powerflex-connector-conf-file
    7. Edit the OpenStackControlplane CR and update the Cinder backend parameter with the PowerFlex details: 
      oc edit openstackcontrolplane
      1. Modify the cinderVolumes section as follows: 
        … <truncated>
        	cinderVolumes:
                powerflex:
                  customServiceConfig: |
                    [powerflex]
        volume_driver = cinder.volume.drivers.dell_emc.powerflex.driver.PowerFlexDriver
                    volume_backend_name = powerflex
                    powerflex_storage_pools = PD-1:SP-SSD-1
                  customServiceConfigSecrets:
                  - cinder-volume-powerflex-secrets
                  networkAttachments:
                  - storage
                  replicas: 1
                  resources: {}
        	… <truncated>
      2. In the extraMounts section, update specifications such as the mount path, connector file name, and volume propagation for the PowerFlex storage usage: 
        … <truncated>
        spec:
          extraMounts:
          - extraVol:
            - extraVolType: powerflex
              mounts:
              - mountPath: /opt/emc/scaleio/openstack
                name: powerflex-connector
                readOnly: true
              propagation:
              - CinderVolume
              volumes:
              - name: powerflex-connector
                secret:
                  secretName: powerflex-connector-conf-files
            name: v1
            region: r1
         … <truncated>
      3. Save and exit the file, ensuring the following output: 
        openstackcontrolplane.core.openstack.org/openstack-control-edited
    8. Verify that the Cinder pod for PowerFlex is up and running: 
      oc get pods -n openstack | grep powerflex
      					cinder-volume-powerflex-0                                      2/2     Running     0              41d

PowerFlex with RHOSO configuration

  • Install the PowerFlex SDC package

    Install and configure the SDC driver on all control plane and data plane nodes. This is necessary for Glance and Nova services to expose PowerFlex volumes as block devices to the application that resides on the data plane.

    Perform the following steps:

    1. Before proceeding with the SDC installation, ensure that the PowerFlex data1 and data2 networks have been configured.
    2. Copy the PowerFlex SDC and LIA packages to both the control plane and data plane nodes and install them: 
      $ MDM_IP=<IPaddress> rpm -ivh EMC-ScaleIO-sdc-<build_version>.x86_64 
      $ TOKEN=<password> rpm -ivh EMC-ScaleIO-lia-<build_version>.x86_64
    3. Verify that the SDC hosts are mapped to the PowerFlex cluster by performing the following steps:
      • Log in to the primary MDM and query all SDCs. The MDM lists all the control plane and data plane nodes on which you have installed the SDC. Verify the connectivity and availability:
        $ scli --login --management_system_ip <powerflex_manager_ip> --username admin --password <password> 
        $ scli --query_all_sdc
      • Alternatively, log in to the PowerFlex Manager UI. Select Block > Hostsand verify that the data plane nodes are listed

PowerFlex with RHOSO configuration

  • Creating a backend volume

    Configure the backend volume using the Horizon dashboard that interacts with the volume type interface, which is mapped to the backend configuration that is defined in the cinder.conf file. Perform the following steps:
    1. Create a new Cinder volume type to be mapped to the storage back-end driver:
      1. Log in to Horizon using the admin credentials you obtained in Enable and verify Horizon access.
      2. Click the Admin tab on the upper left side and select Volume Type from the Volume drop-down menu.
    2. Select Create Volume Type.
    3. Update the required name and description, and then click Create Volume Type.
    4. Create the extra specs parameter for newly created volumes. To do this:
      1. Select New Volume Type > View Extra Specs from the drop-down menu.
      2. Click Create and update the value of the volume_backend_name key to powerflex. Ensure that this value is same as the volume backend name that is specified in the Cinder configuration file.
    5. Verify that the volume_backend_name value is updated successfully.

Red Hat OpenStack Services on OpenShift

  • Red Hat OpenStack Services on OpenShift (RHOSO) 18 is a solution that integrates OpenStack's cloud infrastructure with OpenShift's container orchestration platform. This allows users to manage both virtualized resources and containerized applications in a unified environment. RHOSO combines OpenStack’s IaaS capabilities with OpenShift's Kubernetes-based application management, providing a scalable and flexible hybrid cloud solution.

    RHOSO offers substantial improvements over previous versions of Red Hat OpenStack Platform (RHOSP). The RHOSO control plane is natively hosted on RHOCP, and the external RHEL-based data plane and workloads are managed with Ansible.

    For more information, see Red Hat OpenStack Services on OpenShift.

RHOSO setup verification

  • Verify that the internal service endpoints are registered with each service from the openstackclient pod. The plane creates an openstackclient pod that you can access through a remote shell (rsh) to run OpenStack CLI commands.

    1. Open a remote shell connection to the openstackclient pod:
      oc rsh -n openstack openstackclient
    2. Run the following command:
      sh-5.1$ openstack endpoint list

Solution validation

  • To perform storage operations, ensure that the PowerFlex cluster is healthy and has been configured to work with OpenStack using the Dell CSI driver. This check is necessary because all storage requests from RHOSO communicate through the REST API using the PowerFlex Manager IP address. To verify that the OpenStack deployment has been successfully completed, perform the following checks:

    • Verify PowerFlex connectivity.
    • Verify control and data plane status.
    • Verify that the volume type is created to use the PowerFlex storage backend.

Storage planning

  • Planning the storage for RHOSO deployment is important for infrastructure teams. To choose an optimal storage system, start the process by assessing current storage needs, projecting future requirements based on business growth.

    In this solution, the PowerFlex system is used for storage operations. The system is deployed in a two-layer configuration, consisting of four storage nodes. RHOSO uses the Cinder driver to provision and manage PowerFlex storage volumes.

    For complete information about deployment configurations, see "Dell PowerFlex Software: Technical Documentation" in References.

Testing Cinder operations

  • The Cinder driver is designed and tested to work with the PowerFlex storage backend. Perform the following steps for PowerFlex volume creation from OpenStack Horizon:
    1. Log in to Horizon using the admin credentials.
    2. On the Project tab, click Volume.
    3. Select Create Volume and update the following fields as required: Volume Name, Description, Volume Source, Type (select created Volume Type), Size (in multiples of 8 GB), and Availability Zone (select Nova).
    4. Verify that the new volume is created in the PowerFlex and ensure that users can perform the following operations in the Horizon dashboard:
      • Attach/detach the volume to an instance. The following table lists validation operations.
      • Create multiple volumes for different projects.
    For more information, see Cinder Administration.

    The following table lists validation operations:

    Table 5. Validated Cinder functionality with PowerFlex
    Features/Functions Dell PowerFlex
    Create/delete volume Yes
    Attach/detach volume Yes
    Extend/resize volume Yes
    Create/delete and attach/detach snapshot Yes
    Create volume from snapshot Yes
    Create boot volume/snapshot from boot volume Yes
    Create volume from volume Yes
    Create image from volume Yes
    Extend attached volume Yes
    Thin and thick provisioning Yes
    Volume migration Yes
    Multi-attach support Yes
    Note: To verify Nova, Glance, or operations that are related to other OpenStack services through the Horizon dashboard, see OpenStack Dashboard User Documentation.

YAML file for data plane deployment

  • openstack-edpm-node-set.yaml 


    apiVersion: dataplane.openstack.org/v1beta1
    kind: OpenStackDataplaneNodeSet
    metadata:
      name: openstack-data-plane
      namespace: openstack
    spec:
      env:
        - name: ANSIBLE_FORCE_COLOR
          value: "True"
      preProvisioned: true
      nodes:
          edpm-compute1:
            hostName: edpm-compute1
            ansible:
              ansibleHost: 172.17.170.30
            networks:
            - name: CtlPlane
              subnetName: subnet1
              defaultRoute: false
              fixedIP: 172.17.163.90
            - name: InternalApi
              subnetName: subnet1
            - name: Storage
              subnetName: subnet1
            - name: Tenant
              subnetName: subnet1
          edpm-compute2:
            hostName: edpm-compute2
            ansible:
              ansibleHost: 172.17.170.31
            networks:
            - name: CtlPlane
              subnetName: subnet1
              defaultRoute: false
              fixedIP: 172.17.163.91
            - name: InternalApi
              subnetName: subnet1
            - name: Storage
              subnetName: subnet1
            - name: Tenant
              subnetName: subnet1
      networkAttachments:
        - ctlplane
      nodeTemplate:
        ansibleSSHPrivateKeySecret: dataplane-ansible-ssh-private-key-secret
        extraMounts:
          - extraVolType: Logs
            volumes:
            - name: ansible-logs
              persistentVolumeClaim:
                claimName: dataplane-ansible-logs
            mounts:
            - name: ansible-logs
              mountPath: "/runner/artifacts"
        managementNetwork: ctlplane
        ansible:
          ansibleUser: cloud-admin
          ansiblePort: 22
          ansibleVarsFrom:
            - prefix: subscription_manager_
              secretRef:
                name: subscription-manager
            - secretRef:
                name: red hat-registry
          ansibleVars:
            edpm_network_config_os_net_config_mappings:
              edpm-compute1:
                # Map nic1 to eno1/enp1s0f0
                nic1: "9c:63:c0:95:b4:65"
              edpm-compute2:
                # Map nic1 to eno1/enp1s0f0
                nic1: "9c:63:c0:95:b4:0d"
            edpm_bootstrap_command: |
              subscription-manager register --username {{ 'vivekanandan.k@dell.com' }} --password {{ 'Vivek100192' }}
              subscription-manager release --set=9.4
              subscription-manager repos --disable=*
              subscription-manager repos --enable=rhel-9-for-x86_64-baseos-eus-rpms --enable=rhel-9-for-x86_64-appstream-eus-rpms --enable=rhel-9-for-x86_64-highavailability-eus-rpms --enable=fast-datapath-for-rhel-9-x86_64-rpms --enable=rhoso-18.0-for-rhel-9-x86_64-rpms --enable=rhceph-7-tools-for-rhel-9-x86_64-rpms
            edpm_bootstrap_release_version_package: []
            neutron_physical_bridge_name: br-ex
            neutron_public_interface_name: eno2np1.170
            service_net_map:
              nova_api_network: internal_api
              nova_libvirt_network: internal_api
            edpm_chrony_ntp_servers:
              - 172.17.170.5
            # edpm_network_config
            # Default nic config template for a EDPM compute node
            # These vars are edpm_network_config role vars
            edpm_network_config_template: |
              ---
              {% set mtu_list = [ctlplane_mtu] %}
              {% for network in nodeset_networks %}
              {{ mtu_list.append(lookup('vars', networks_lower[network] ~ '_mtu')) }}
              {%- endfor %}
              {% set min_viable_mtu = mtu_list | max %}
              network_config:
              - type: ovs_bridge
                name: {{ neutron_physical_bridge_name }}
                mtu: {{ min_viable_mtu }}
                use_dhcp: false
                dns_servers: {{ ctlplane_dns_nameservers }}
                  #domain: {{ dns_search_domains }}
                addresses:
                - ip_netmask: {{ ctlplane_ip }}/{{ ctlplane_cidr }}
                routes: {{ ctlplane_host_routes }}
                members:
                - type: interface
                  name: nic1
                  mtu: {{ min_viable_mtu }}
                  # force the MAC address of the bridge to this interface
                  primary: true
              {% for network in nodeset_networks %}
                - type: vlan
                  mtu: {{ lookup('vars', networks_lower[network] ~ '_mtu') }}
                  vlan_id: {{ lookup('vars', networks_lower[network] ~ '_vlan_id') }}
                  addresses:
                  - ip_netmask:
                      {{ lookup('vars', networks_lower[network] ~ '_ip') }}/{{ lookup('vars', networks_lower[network] ~ '_cidr') }}
                  routes: {{ lookup('vars', networks_lower[network] ~ '_host_routes') }}
              {% endfor %}
            ctlplane_dns_nameservers:
            - 10.228.254.66
            - 172.17.170.1
